trivial

/TRIV-ee-uhl/ · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Trivial means of so little importance or significance that it barely deserves attention.

The two delegations nearly stalled the peace talks over a trivial question: the exact shape of the negotiating table.

Example

When the school newspaper staff met to cover the flooded gymnasium, one member kept steering the discussion toward which color of staples to use for the print edition. The editor gently reminded him that staple color was trivial next to a story affecting the whole school.

Staple color has almost no importance compared to the flood story, which is exactly what makes it trivial.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

trifling: Trifling means so small or unimportant that it can be waved away: a trifling sum, a trifling objection. It is a slightly old-fashioned, dismissive word. Trivial is its everyday partner: a trivial matter barely deserves attention, and calling it trivial says so plainly.

insignificant: Insignificant means too small to matter or to leave any real mark, and it can describe amounts, effects, or people. Trivial aims specifically at importance: a trivial question or detail is one that does not deserve the attention it is getting, whatever its size.

petty: Petty means small-minded as well as small: petty complaints and petty rules concern trifles, and the word quietly criticizes the person fussing over them. Trivial judges only the matter itself; a trivial detail is unimportant, but calling it trivial sneers at no one.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

crucial: extremely important or decisive

momentous: of great importance or consequence

Where it sits · how much it actually matters — minor → trivial → meaningless

minor vs. trivial: A minor issue still matters a little, while a trivial one is so unimportant that it barely deserves attention at all.

meaningless vs. trivial: A trivial detail has almost no importance, but a meaningless one has no significance whatsoever, no matter how closely you look.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — tri-

Root — tri-: three

Root — via

Root — via: from Latin via, road or way

Suffix — -al

Suffix — -al: adjective-forming ending

Put it together

Put it together: Trivial comes from Latin trivium, 'a place where three roads meet,' built from tri-, 'three,' and via, 'road,' plus the adjective ending -al. A busy crossroads was where people swapped ordinary, everyday chatter, so trivialis came to mean 'commonplace,' and from there the word drifted to 'unimportant.'

Use the root in a new word: trivia

Use the root in a new word: trivia: Friday night trivia rewards players who remember small, commonplace facts, and the word comes from the same Latin trivium, the three-way crossroads where travelers once traded everyday small talk.

Word Building

Word Choice

neutral

Trivial is about importance, not size: a trivial error can be physically large, and a tiny object can be far from trivial. It often appears in the phrases 'trivial matter,' 'trivial detail,' and the dismissive 'merely trivial.'
